label: thm:intro-main
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:intro-main}
Let $\Lambda$ be a finite-dimensional algebra over any field. If
$P_i\twoheadrightarrow S_i$, $1\le i\le r$, are the projective
covers of its pairwise nonisomorphic simple modules, put
$d_\Lambda=\sum_{i=1}^r\bigl(\ell_\Lambda(P_i)-1\bigr).$
For every torsion pair there is $0\le N\le d_\Lambda$ such that the functor
$G^{(m)}$ is a triangle equivalence for all $m\ge2N+1$.
head: environment

label: thm:intro-calculus
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:intro-calculus}
Let $\mathbf{P}=[P^{-1}\xrightarrow d P^0]$ be two-term silting
and let $(I_n)$ be the HRS ideal filtration of its torsion pair.
Put $\mathbf{P}_n=\mathbf{P}\otimes_\Lambda\Lambda_n$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item The complex $\mathbf{P}_n$ is silting and induces the transported pair.
The ideal $I_{n+1}/I_n$ is generated by the matrix coefficients of
\[
\{H: P_n^0\to P_n^{-1}\mid Hd_n=d_nH=0\},
\]
where $d_n$ is the reduced differential and
$P_n^{-1}=P^{-1}/P^{-1}I_n$,
$ P_n^0= P^0/ P^0I_n$.
\item With $R_n=H^{-1}(\mathbf{P})\cap P^{-1}I_n$, one has
$H^{-1}(\mathbf{P}_n)=H^{-1}(\mathbf{P})/R_n$ and
\[
h_\Lambda(\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{P}))=
\min\{n:\operatorname{Hom}_\Lambda(H^0(\mathbf{P}),H^{-1}(\mathbf{P})/R_n)=0\}.
\]
The quotient $\Lambda/I_\infty$ is the largest quotient over which
the reduction of $\mathbf{P}$ is tilting.
\item Let $h_{\mathrm{ev}}$ and $h_{\mathrm{odd}}$ be the HRS
heights of the two parity towers. The least $s\ge1$ for which every
$G^{(m)}$, $m\ge s$, is an equivalence is
\[
\sigma_\Lambda(\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{P}))=h_{\mathrm{ev}}+h_{\mathrm{odd}}+1,
\qquad h_{\mathrm{odd}}\le h_{\mathrm{ev}}\le h_{\mathrm{odd}}+1.
\]
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

label: thm:intro-examples
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:intro-examples}
	Let $k$ be a field and let $c_0\ge c_1\ge\cdots\ge c_{N-1}>0$ be
	integers, with $N\ge1$. 
	\begin{enumerate}
	\item There exist a finite-dimensional basic
	$k$-algebra $\Lambda$ with two simple modules and Loewy length three,
	and a basic two-term silting complex $\mathbf{P}$, such that
	\[
	\dim_k\Lambda=4+4\sum_{m=0}^{N-1}c_m,\qquad
	h_\Lambda(\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{P}))=N.
	\]
	\item For its HRS ideal filtration $\{I_m\}$, put $\Lambda_m=\Lambda/I_m$
	and $\mathbf{P}_m=\mathbf{P}\otimes_\Lambda\Lambda_m$. Then, for $0\le m<N$,
	\[
	\dim_k(I_{m+1}/I_m)=4c_m,\qquad
	\dim_k\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm K^{\mathrm b}(\operatorname{proj}\Lambda_m)}(\mathbf{P}_m,\mathbf{P}_m[-1])=2c_m.
	\]
	\end{enumerate}
head: environment

label: prop:chz
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:chz}
Let $G:\mathrm D^{\mathrm b}(\mathcal{B})\to\mathrm D^{\mathrm b}(\mathcal{A})$ be a realization functor.
Its restriction $G|_{\mathcal{A}'}:\mathcal{A}'\to\mathcal{A}$ is exact and fully faithful.
It identifies the induced torsion pair with $(\mathcal{T},\mathcal{F})$.
The following conditions are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $G$ is an equivalence.
\item $G|_{\mathcal{A}'}$ is an equivalence.
\item The essential image of $G|_{\mathcal{A}'}$ is $\mathcal{A}$.
\end{enumerate}
In this case every realization functor for the associated backward
tilt is also an equivalence.
head: environment
name: Propositions 3.1--3.3

label: def:iterative
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:iterative}
Start with $\mathcal{A}^{(0)}=\mathcal{A}$ and the torsion pair $(\mathcal{T},\mathcal{F})$.
Form $\mathcal{A}^{(2n+1)}$ by the forward tilt of $\mathcal{A}^{(2n)}$.
Then form $\mathcal{A}^{(2n+2)}$ by the associated backward tilt, with
its induced torsion pair. Each heart is formed in the bounded
derived category of the preceding heart. Denote the chosen
realization functors by
\[
G^{(m)}:\mathrm D^{\mathrm b}(\mathcal{A}^{(m)})\longrightarrow\mathrm D^{\mathrm b}(\mathcal{A}^{(m-1)}),
\qquad m\ge1.
\]
head: environment

label: lem:same-simples
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:same-simples}
An exact full abelian subcategory $\mathcal{C}\subseteq\mathcal{A}$ containing all
$S_i$ is closed under subobjects and quotients in $\mathcal{A}$.
It is a length category with exactly the simple objects
$S_1,\ldots,S_r$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $Y\subseteq X$ in $\mathcal{A}$, with $X\in\mathcal{C}$. A composition series
of $X/Y$ lifts to a chain
\[
X=X_0\supset X_1\supset\cdots\supset X_s=Y
\]
with simple successive factors. If $X_j\in\mathcal{C}$, then
$X_j\twoheadrightarrow X_j/X_{j+1}$ is a morphism in $\mathcal{C}$.
Since the inclusion is exact, its kernel $X_{j+1}$ belongs to $\mathcal{C}$.
Induction gives $Y\in\mathcal{C}$, and the cokernel of $Y\hookrightarrow X$
gives $X/Y\in\mathcal{C}$.

It follows that every composition series in $\mathcal{A}$ of an object of
$\mathcal{C}$ is also a composition series in $\mathcal{C}$. Thus $\mathcal{C}$ is a length
category with simple objects $S_1,\ldots,S_r$.
head: environment

label: prop:internal-covers
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:internal-covers}\label{cor:proj-generator}
Let $\mathcal{C}\subseteq\mathcal{A}$ be an exact full abelian subcategory containing all $S_i$.
Every $S_i$ has a projective cover
$q_i^\mathcal{C}:Q_i^\mathcal{C}\twoheadrightarrow S_i$ in $\mathcal{C}$, with $Q_i^\mathcal{C}$
a quotient of $P_i$ in $\mathcal{A}$. The object
$Q^\mathcal{C}=\bigoplus_iQ_i^\mathcal{C}$ is a projective generator.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $S_i\in\mathcal{C}$ and quotient lengths are bounded by
$\ell_\mathcal{A}(P_i)$, we may choose an epimorphism
$u:P_i\twoheadrightarrow Q$ with $Q\in\mathcal{C}$ of maximal length among
the quotients of $P_i$ lying in $\mathcal{C}$. Let
$f:P_i\to X$, where $X\in\mathcal{C}$, and put
$Y=\operatorname{Im}(u,f)\subseteq Q\oplus X$. By
Lemma~\ref{lem:same-simples}, $Y\in\mathcal{C}$. The projection
$p:Y\twoheadrightarrow Q$ is an epimorphism. Since $Y$ is a
quotient of $P_i$, maximality gives
\[
\ell_\mathcal{A}(Q)\le\ell_\mathcal{A}(Y)\le\ell_\mathcal{A}(Q).
\]
Thus $p$ is an isomorphism and $f$ factors uniquely through $u$.
We obtain a natural isomorphism
\[
\operatorname{Hom}_\mathcal{C}(Q,-)\simeq\operatorname{Hom}_\mathcal{A}(P_i,-)|_\mathcal{C}.
\]
Since $P_i$ is projective and the inclusion $\mathcal{C}\hookrightarrow\mathcal{A}$
is exact, this functor is exact. Hence $Q$ is projective in $\mathcal{C}$.

The kernel of the projective cover $\pi_i$ is the unique maximal
subobject of $P_i$. Since $Q\ne0$, we have
$\ker u\subseteq\ker\pi_i$. Thus $\pi_i$ induces
$q:Q\twoheadrightarrow S_i$. Every proper subobject of $Q$ is
contained in $\ker q=(\ker\pi_i)/(\ker u)$. Thus $q$ is
an essential epimorphism, and hence a projective cover in $\mathcal{C}$.

Set $Q_i^\mathcal{C}=Q$. Since $\mathcal{C}$ is a length category and every simple
object is a quotient of one of the $Q_i^\mathcal{C}$, induction on length
shows that $Q^\mathcal{C}$ is a projective generator.
head: environment

title: Corollary
body_md:
Every $X\in\mathcal{C}$ has a presentation $Q_1\to Q_0\to X\to0$
with $Q_0,Q_1\in\operatorname{add} Q^\mathcal{C}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For $X\ne0$ in $\mathcal{C}$, choose an exact sequence
$0\to K\to X\to S_i\to0$. Projectivity lifts $q_i^\mathcal{C}$ to
$Q_i^\mathcal{C}\to X$, and induction on length gives an epimorphism
$Q'\twoheadrightarrow K$ with $Q'\in\operatorname{add} Q^\mathcal{C}$. The induced map
$Q'\oplus Q_i^\mathcal{C}\to X$ is epic. Applying this construction to
its kernel gives the required presentation.
head: environment

label: prop:strict-mu
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:strict-mu}
Set $\mu_\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{C})=\sum_i\ell_\mathcal{A}(Q_i^\mathcal{C})$.
If $\mathcal{C}'\subseteq\mathcal{C}$ are exact full abelian subcategories containing
all $S_i$, then $\mu_\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{C}')\le\mu_\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{C})$.
Equality holds if and only if $\mathcal{C}'=\mathcal{C}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $q_i^{\mathcal{C}'}:Q_i^{\mathcal{C}'}\twoheadrightarrow S_i$ is an
epimorphism in $\mathcal{C}$, projectivity gives
$f_i:Q_i^\mathcal{C}\to Q_i^{\mathcal{C}'}$ such that
$q_i^{\mathcal{C}'}f_i=q_i^\mathcal{C}$. The subobject $\operatorname{Im} f_i$ belongs to
$\mathcal{C}'$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:same-simples} and maps onto $S_i$.
Since $q_i^{\mathcal{C}'}$ is essential, $\operatorname{Im} f_i=Q_i^{\mathcal{C}'}$. Therefore
\[
\ell_\mathcal{A}(Q_i^{\mathcal{C}'})\le\ell_\mathcal{A}(Q_i^\mathcal{C})
\quad\text{for every }i,
\]
which proves the inequality.

If $\mu_\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{C}')=\mu_\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{C})$, each epimorphism $f_i$ has
source and target of equal length and is therefore an isomorphism.
The two categories have a common projective generator $Q$. For
$X\in\mathcal{C}$, take a presentation $Q_1\to Q_0\to X\to0$ with
$Q_0,Q_1\in\operatorname{add} Q$. Since $\mathcal{C}'$ is full and its inclusion is
exact, the cokernel of $Q_1\to Q_0$ belongs to $\mathcal{C}'$. Thus
$X\in\mathcal{C}'$ and $\mathcal{C}=\mathcal{C}'$. The converse is immediate.
head: environment

label: thm:categorical-finite-height
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:categorical-finite-height} 
Put $d_\mathcal{A}=\sum_{i=1}^r\bigl(\ell_\mathcal{A}(P_i)-1\bigr)$.
Let $\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{C}_0\supsetneq\mathcal{C}_1\supsetneq\cdots\supsetneq\mathcal{C}_s$
be a strictly descending chain of exact full abelian subcategories
containing all $S_i$. Then $s\le d_\mathcal{A}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Proposition~\ref{prop:strict-mu}, $\mu_\mathcal{A}$ decreases by at
least one at each inclusion. Since every $Q_i^{\mathcal{C}_s}$ is nonzero,
$\mu_\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{C}_s)\ge r$. It follows that
$s\le\mu_\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{A})-\mu_\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{C}_s)
\le d_\mathcal{A}.$
head: environment

label: prop:absorption
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $\mathcal{C}_{n+1}=\mathcal{C}_n$, the fully faithful functor $E_n$ is
an equivalence. Proposition~\ref{prop:chz} implies that
$G^{(2n+1)}$ and $G^{(2n+2)}$ are equivalences.

The functor $E_n$ identifies the torsion pairs on $\mathcal{A}^{(2n+2)}$
and $\mathcal{A}^{(2n)}$. Hence its derived equivalence restricts to an
equivalence of their forward HRS hearts,
$\mathcal{A}^{(2n+3)}\simeq\mathcal{A}^{(2n+1)}$. Transporting $G^{(2n+1)}$
along these equivalences gives an equivalence realization functor
for the forward tilt of $\mathcal{A}^{(2n+2)}$. By
\cite[Corollary 2.8]{CHZ}, the chosen realization $G^{(2n+3)}$
is also an equivalence. Proposition~\ref{prop:chz} then gives
$\mathcal{C}_{n+2}=\mathcal{C}_{n+1}$ and shows that $G^{(2n+4)}$ is an
equivalence. Induction completes the proof.
head: environment

label: thm:categorical-extension
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:categorical-extension}
For every torsion pair in $\mathcal{A}$, there is $0\le N\le d_\mathcal{A}$
such that $\mathcal{C}_n=\mathcal{C}_N$ for $n\ge N$.
Every $G^{(m)}$ with $m\ge2N+1$ is an equivalence.
In particular, the result applies to $\mathcal{A}=\operatorname{mod}\Lambda$ for any
finite-dimensional algebra $\Lambda$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If $\mathcal{C}_{n+1}\ne\mathcal{C}_n$ for all $0\le n\le d_\mathcal{A}$, the first
$d_\mathcal{A}+1$ inclusions would be strict.
This contradicts Theorem~\ref{thm:categorical-finite-height}.
Thus equality occurs at some $N\le d_\mathcal{A}$.
Proposition~\ref{prop:absorption} gives the conclusion.
head: environment

label: prop:quotient-description
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:quotient-description}
Every exact full abelian subcategory $\mathcal{C}\subseteq\operatorname{mod}\Lambda$
containing all simple modules has the form
\[
\mathcal{C}=\{X:XI_\mathcal{C}=0\}=\operatorname{mod}(\Lambda/I_\mathcal{C}),\qquad
I_\mathcal{C}=\operatorname{Ann}_\Lambda\mathcal{C}\subseteq\operatorname{rad}\Lambda.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Put $I=I_\mathcal{C}$.
Among the finite intersections of annihilators of objects of $\mathcal{C}$,
choose one of minimal dimension. Since intersecting it with
$\operatorname{Ann}_\Lambda Y$ for any $Y\in\mathcal{C}$ cannot reduce its dimension,
it equals $I$.
Choose $X_1,\ldots,X_m\in\mathcal{C}$ realizing this finite intersection,
and put $X=\bigoplus_jX_j$. Then
\[
\operatorname{Ann}_\Lambda X=\bigcap_{j=1}^m\operatorname{Ann}_\Lambda X_j=I.
\]
Since $\operatorname{Ann}_{\Lambda/I}X=\operatorname{Ann}_\Lambda X/I=0$,
$X$ is faithful over $\Lambda/I$.
For a $k$-basis $x_1,\ldots,x_d$ of $X$, consider
\[
\Lambda/I\longrightarrow X^d,\qquad
a+I\longmapsto(x_1a,\ldots,x_da).
\]
Since $Xa=0$ implies $a\in I$, the displayed right
$\Lambda$-module map is injective.

By Lemma~\ref{lem:same-simples}, we have $\Lambda/I\in\mathcal{C}$.
Every finite $\Lambda/I$-module is a quotient of $(\Lambda/I)^r$
for some $r$, so the same lemma gives $\operatorname{mod}(\Lambda/I)\subseteq\mathcal{C}$.
The reverse inclusion follows from the definition of $I$.
Since $\mathcal{C}$ contains every simple module, $I\subseteq\operatorname{rad}\Lambda$.
Finally, $\operatorname{Ann}_\Lambda(\Lambda/I)=I$ gives uniqueness.
head: environment

label: lem:square-zero-annihilator
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(1) Take the torsion sequence
$0\to U\to\Lambda\to V\to0$ of the regular right module.
Since $V\in\mathcal{F}$, the equality $VJ_\mathcal{T}=0$ gives
$J_\mathcal{T}=\Lambda J_\mathcal{T}\subseteq U$.
Since $U\in\mathcal{T}$, we also have $UJ_\mathcal{T}=0$. Thus $J_\mathcal{T}^2\subseteq UJ_\mathcal{T}=0$.
Since $\mathcal{T},\mathcal{F}\subseteq\mathcal{C}_n$, we have $I_n\subseteq J_\mathcal{T}$.

(2) For a $\Lambda_n$-module $X$, the coset $a+I_n$ annihilates $X$
if and only if $Xa=0$. Thus the two annihilators over $\Lambda_n$ are
$\operatorname{Ann}_\Lambda\mathcal{T}/I_n$ and $\operatorname{Ann}_\Lambda\mathcal{F}/I_n$.
Their intersection is $J_{\mathcal{T}}/I_n$.
head: environment

label: def:tau-admissible
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:tau-admissible}
A module $X$ is \emph{$\mathcal{T}$-admissible} if there are submodules
$K_1\subseteq K_2\subseteq E$ and $L\subseteq E$ such that
\[
X\simeq K_2/K_1,\qquad K_2\cap L\in\mathcal{F},\qquad
E/(K_1+L)\in\mathcal{T}.
\]
Write $\operatorname{Adm}_\mathcal{T}(\Lambda)$ for the full subcategory of these modules.
head: environment

label: prop:noohi-admissible
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:noohi-admissible}
One has
$\operatorname{Adm}_\mathcal{T}(\Lambda)=\mathcal{C}_\mathcal{T}=\operatorname{mod}(\Lambda/I_\Lambda(\mathcal{T}))$.
In particular,
$I_\Lambda(\mathcal{T})=\operatorname{Ann}_\Lambda\operatorname{Adm}_\mathcal{T}(\Lambda)$ is intrinsic
to the torsion pair.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By \cite[Section 8.1 and Proposition 8.1]{Noohi}, the second forward
HRS heart is described by diagrams
$[K_1\subseteq K_2\subseteq E\supseteq L]$ satisfying the conditions
of Definition~\ref{def:tau-admissible}.
In $\mathrm D^{\mathrm b}(\mathcal{B})$, this heart has $\mathcal{T}$ in degree $-1$ and $\mathcal{F}[1]$
in degree $0$, so it is $\Sigma_\mathcal{B}\mathcal{A}'$.
After shifting by $\Sigma_\mathcal{B}^{-1}$, the restricted realization
sends such a diagram to $K_2/K_1$.
Its essential image is therefore $\operatorname{Adm}_\mathcal{T}(\Lambda)$.
By Proposition~\ref{prop:chz}, the image is independent of the
realization functor and equals $\mathcal{C}_\mathcal{T}$.
The remaining assertions follow from
Proposition~\ref{prop:quotient-description}.
head: environment

title: Example
body_md:
Let $\Gamma$ be a finite-dimensional algebra and let
	$(\mathcal{T},\mathcal{F})$ be a split torsion pair in $\operatorname{mod}\Gamma$. Every module $X\in\operatorname{mod}\Gamma$ decomposes
	as $X\simeq T\oplus F$ with $T\in\mathcal{T}$ and $F\in\mathcal{F}$.
	In Definition~\ref{def:tau-admissible}, take
	\[
	E=X,\quad K_1=0,\quad K_2=X,\quad L=F.
	\]
	Then
	$K_2/K_1\simeq X$, $K_2\cap L=F\in\mathcal{F}$, and
	$E/(K_1+L)\simeq T\in\mathcal{T}$.
	Thus every $\Gamma$-module is $\mathcal{T}$-admissible,
	and $\operatorname{Adm}_{\mathcal{T}}(\Gamma)=\operatorname{mod}\Gamma.$
	By Proposition~\ref{prop:noohi-admissible},
	\[
	\operatorname{Adm}_{\mathcal{T}}(\Gamma)
	=
	\operatorname{mod}\bigl(\Gamma/I_\Gamma(\mathcal{T})\bigr)
	\]
	as the full subcategory of modules annihilated by
	$I_\Gamma(\mathcal{T})$.  It follows that $I_\Gamma(\mathcal{T})=0$.
head: environment

label: thm:hrs-ideal-recursion
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $\mathcal{C}_{n+1}\subseteq\mathcal{C}_n=\operatorname{mod}\Lambda_n$ is the second-heart
image for $(\mathcal{T}_n,\mathcal{F}_n)$, Proposition~\ref{prop:noohi-admissible} gives
\[
I_{\Lambda_n}(\mathcal{T}_n)=\operatorname{Ann}_{\Lambda_n}\mathcal{C}_{n+1}
=\operatorname{Ann}_{\Lambda_n}\operatorname{mod}(\Lambda/I_{n+1})=I_{n+1}/I_n.
\]
The second equality in \eqref{eq:hrs-ideal-recursion} follows by
taking quotients.

Equivalently, $I_{n+1}$ is the inverse image of
$I_{\Lambda_n}(\mathcal{T}_n)$ under $\Lambda\twoheadrightarrow\Lambda_n$.
Since admissibility depends only on the torsion pair
(Definition~\ref{def:tau-admissible}) and the transported classes
are fixed by restriction of scalars, induction
from $I_0=0$ proves independence of all realization choices.
head: environment

label: rem:ext2-hrs-ideal
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:ext2-hrs-ideal}
For $F\in\mathcal{F}$ and $T\in\mathcal{T}$, put $F'=\Sigma_\mathcal{B}^{-1}(F[1])\in\mathcal{A}'$.
The identification
of first Yoneda extensions in a heart with degree-one morphisms gives
$\operatorname{YExt}^1_{\mathcal{A}'}(F',T)
\simeq\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm D^{\mathrm b}(\mathcal{B})}(F[1],\Sigma_\mathcal{B}^2T)
\simeq\operatorname{YExt}^2_\mathcal{B}(F[1],T)$.
Combining this with the exact equivalence
$\mathcal{A}'\simeq\operatorname{mod}(\Lambda/I_1)$ and the fully faithful embedding of
\cite[Proposition~3.1]{CHZ} gives
\[
\operatorname{YExt}^2_\mathcal{B}(F[1],T)
\simeq\operatorname{Ext}^1_{\Lambda/I_1}(F,T)
\hookrightarrow\operatorname{Ext}^1_\Lambda(F,T).
\]
An extension $0\to T\to X\to F\to0$ lies in this image
exactly when $XI_1=0$.
Indeed, all three terms are then $\Lambda/I_1$-modules and both
maps are $\Lambda/I_1$-linear. Since any $\Lambda$-linear equivalence between
two such extensions is also $\Lambda/I_1$-linear, restriction of
scalars is injective on extension classes.
head: environment

label: def:three-invariants
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:three-invariants}
The \emph{HRS height} is
$h_\Lambda(\mathcal{T})=\min\{n\ge0:I_{n+1}=I_n\}$.
For $h=h_\Lambda(\mathcal{T})$, write $I_\infty=I_h$ for the stable
ideal.
head: environment

label: cor:first-hrs-ideal-stopping
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Theorem~\ref{thm:hrs-ideal-recursion} and
Proposition~\ref{prop:quotient-description}, we have that
\[I_{\Lambda_n}(\mathcal{T}_n)=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad I_{n+1}=I_n
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\mathcal{C}_{n+1}=\mathcal{C}_n.
\]
Thus $(1)\Longleftrightarrow (2)$.

By Proposition~\ref{prop:chz}, $\mathcal{C}_{n+1}=\mathcal{C}_n$ if and only if
$G^{(2n+1)}$ is an equivalence. Thus $(1)\Longleftrightarrow (3)$.
By Proposition~\ref{prop:absorption}, if $I_{n+1}=I_n$, then $I_n=I_m$ for any $m>n$.
head: environment

title: Corollary
body_md:
The HRS height of a torsion pair $(\mathcal{T},\mathcal{F})$ in $\operatorname{mod}\Lambda$ satisfies
	\[
	h_\Lambda(\mathcal{T})\le
	\min\{d_\Lambda,\ell_{\Lambda^{\mathrm e}}(J_\mathcal{T})\}.
	\]
	Moreover,
	$\ell_{\Lambda^{\mathrm e}}(J_\mathcal{T})\le\ell_\Lambda(J_\mathcal{T})
	\le d_\Lambda$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Theorem~\ref{thm:categorical-extension} gives
$h_\Lambda(\mathcal{T})\le d_\Lambda$.
Before stabilization, we have a chain of bimodules
\[
0=I_0\subsetneq I_1\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq I_h\subseteq J_\mathcal{T}
\]
whose first $h$ inclusions are strict. Hence
$h\le\ell_{\Lambda^{\mathrm e}}(J_\mathcal{T})$.
Since $J_\mathcal{T}^2=0$, we have $J_\mathcal{T}\subseteq\operatorname{rad}\Lambda$.
Every strict bimodule chain is also a strict right-module chain, so
$\ell_{\Lambda^{\mathrm e}}(J_\mathcal{T})\le\ell_\Lambda(J_\mathcal{T})
\le\ell_\Lambda(\operatorname{rad}\Lambda)$.
Finally, the regular module decomposes as
$\Lambda_\Lambda\simeq\bigoplus_iP_i$.
Its radical therefore has length
$\sum_i(\ell_\Lambda(P_i)-1)=d_\Lambda$.
head: environment

label: prop:hrs-filtration-tail
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{prop:hrs-filtration-tail}
Restarting the construction at $(\Lambda_s,\mathcal{T}_s)$ gives ideals
$I_{s+n}/I_s$.
This follows by induction from Theorem \ref{thm:hrs-ideal-recursion}.
Since the original filtration is strict before its height and
constant thereafter, the new height is
\[
h_{\Lambda_s}(\mathcal{T}_s)=\max\{h_\Lambda(\mathcal{T})-s,0\}.
\]
In particular, the stable category is
$\operatorname{mod}(\Lambda/I_\infty)$ and its first HRS ideal is zero.
Its common annihilator is $J_\mathcal{T}/I_\infty$ by
Lemma \ref{lem:square-zero-annihilator}.
Note that the equality $I_{\Lambda/I_\infty}(\mathcal{T}_h)=0$ need not imply
$J_\mathcal{T}/I_\infty=0$.
head: environment

label: prop:hrs-height-product
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:hrs-height-product}
Let $\Lambda=\Lambda^{(a)}\times\Lambda^{(b)}$.
Every torsion pair decomposes uniquely into torsion pairs
$(\mathcal{T}^{(a)},\mathcal{F}^{(a)})$ and $(\mathcal{T}^{(b)},\mathcal{F}^{(b)})$ on the two factors.
If their HRS ideal filtrations are $(I_n^{(a)})$ and $(I_n^{(b)})$, then
\[
I_n=I_n^{(a)}\times I_n^{(b)},\qquad
h_\Lambda(\mathcal{T})=
\max\{h_{\Lambda^{(a)}}(\mathcal{T}^{(a)}),
       h_{\Lambda^{(b)}}(\mathcal{T}^{(b)})\}.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The central idempotents of the product decompose every module
into its two components. Since torsion and torsion-free classes
are closed under finite direct sums and summands, they decompose
uniquely as asserted.
Since submodules, intersections, sums, and quotients are computed
componentwise, Definition~\ref{def:tau-admissible} gives
\[
\operatorname{Adm}_\mathcal{T}(\Lambda)=
\operatorname{Adm}_{\mathcal{T}^{(a)}}(\Lambda^{(a)})\times
\operatorname{Adm}_{\mathcal{T}^{(b)}}(\Lambda^{(b)}).
\]
Taking annihilators proves the formula for $I_1$.
Induction using \eqref{eq:hrs-ideal-recursion} gives the formula
for $I_n$. The product filtration is constant precisely when both
factor filtrations are constant, which gives the height formula.
head: environment

label: prop:hereditary-arbitrary-pair
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\mathcal{B}$ be the first HRS heart.
Since $\Lambda$ is hereditary, the usual identification of
extensions in a heart gives, for $T\in\mathcal{T}$ and $F\in\mathcal{F}$,
\[
 \operatorname{Ext}^1_\mathcal{B}(T,F[1])
 \simeq\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm D^{\mathrm b}(\Lambda)}(T,F[2])
 =\operatorname{Ext}^2_\Lambda(T,F)=0.
\]
Thus every torsion sequence for $(\mathcal{F}[1],\mathcal{T})$ splits, and every
object of $\mathcal{B}$ is a direct sum of objects from $\mathcal{F}[1]$ and $\mathcal{T}$.
By \cite[Example~4.2(2)]{CHZ}, the realization for the forward tilt of
$\mathcal{B}$ at $(\mathcal{F}[1],\mathcal{T})$ is an equivalence. Since $\mathcal{A}^{(2)}$ is this
heart shifted by $\Sigma_\mathcal{B}^{-1}$, $G^{(2)}$ is also an equivalence.
Under this equivalence, the forward tilt of $\mathcal{A}^{(2)}$ identifies
with the standard heart $\mathcal{B}$. Hence $G^{(3)}$ is an equivalence by
\cite[Corollary~2.8]{CHZ}, and Theorem~\ref{thm:refined-height}
gives $h_\Lambda(\mathcal{T})\le1$.
head: environment

label: cor:first-hrs-ideal-silting
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{cor:first-hrs-ideal-silting}
The first HRS ideal satisfies
$I_\Lambda(\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{P}))=\mathfrak b_\Lambda(\mathbf{P})$.
Moreover, $\mathfrak b_\Lambda(\mathbf{P})=0$ if and only if $\mathbf{P}$ is tilting.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{P})$ (resp. $\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{Q})$) denote the forward HRS heart associated to $\mathbf{P}$ (resp. $\mathbf{Q}$). The equivalence
\[
 \operatorname{Hom}(\mathbf{P},-):\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{P})\xrightarrow{\sim}\operatorname{mod}\Gamma
\]
takes the torsion pair $(\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{P})[1],\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{P}))$ on $\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{P})$
to $(\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{Q}),\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{Q}))$
by \cite[Theorem~2.3 and Proposition~3.8]{BZ}.
Thus the backward second heart identifies with
$\mathcal H=\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{Q})[-1]\subseteq\mathrm D^{\mathrm b}(\Gamma)$, and the heart
equivalence for $\mathbf{Q}$ gives
\[
 \Psi:\mathcal H\xrightarrow{\sim}\operatorname{mod}\Lambda',\quad
\Psi(X)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm D(\Gamma)}(\mathbf{Q},X[1]).
\]

To compute the image of $\mathcal H$ in $\operatorname{mod}\Lambda$, set
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 E=\tau_{\le0}\operatorname{End}_{\mathrm{dg},\Lambda}(\mathbf{P}),\qquad
 p:E\longrightarrow H^0(E)=\Gamma,\\
 F=\mathbf R\operatorname{Hom}_\Lambda(\mathbf{P},-):\mathrm D(\Lambda)
 \xrightarrow{\sim}\mathrm D(E).
 \end{gathered}
\]
Here $\mathrm D(-)$ denotes the unbounded derived category.
The truncation $\tau_{\le0}$ denotes the good dg truncation.
Since $\mathbf{P}$ is silting,
$H^{>0}\operatorname{End}_{\mathrm{dg},\Lambda}(\mathbf{P})=0$. Hence the natural inclusion
$E\hookrightarrow\operatorname{End}_{\mathrm{dg},\Lambda}(\mathbf{P})$ is a quasi-isomorphism.
Since $\mathbf{P}$ is a compact generator, derived Morita theory gives
the equivalence $F$ \cite[Section~6.1]{Keller}.
Write $p^*=-\otimes_E^{\mathbf L}\Gamma$ for extension of scalars
and $p_*$ for restriction of scalars.

Put $G_0=F^{-1}p_*\colon\mathrm D(\Gamma)\to\mathrm D(\Lambda)$.
Fix $X\in\mathrm D^{\mathrm b}(\Gamma)$. The full subcategory of objects
$Y\in\mathrm D(E)$ for which
$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm D(E)}(Y,p_*X[j])$ is finite-dimensional for every $j$
and vanishes for all but finitely many $j$ is thick.
It contains $E$, since
$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm D(E)}(E,p_*X[j])\simeq H^j(X)$.
Since $F(\Lambda)\in\operatorname{thick}(E)$, the groups
\[
 H^j(G_0X)\simeq\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm D(E)}(F(\Lambda),p_*X[j])
\]
are also finite-dimensional and vanish for all but finitely
many $j$. Hence $G_0$ restricts to
$\mathrm D^{\mathrm b}(\Gamma)\to\mathrm D^{\mathrm b}(\Lambda)$.

On objects with finite-dimensional total cohomology, the standard
heart of $\mathrm D(E)$ is $\operatorname{mod} \Gamma$.
By \cite[Lemma~5.3(a)]{KY}, $F$ restricts to an equivalence
$\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{P})\xrightarrow{\sim}\operatorname{mod}\Gamma$. Since $p_*$ leaves underlying
complexes unchanged, it is $t$-exact and induces the identity
on this standard heart. Thus $G_0$ is $t$-exact
for the corresponding $t$-structures and induces the inverse of
$\operatorname{Hom}(\mathbf{P},-):\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{P})\to\operatorname{mod}\Gamma$. With this identification
of hearts, $G_0$ is a realization functor; see also
\cite[Lemmas~2.13--2.14, Proposition~2.15 and Section~3]{XYZ}.

By \cite[Theorem~4.5 and Remark~4.8]{XYZ},
$\mathbf{Q}\simeq p^*F(\Lambda)[1]$.
Moreover, the induced map
\[
 \Lambda=\operatorname{End}_{\mathrm D(E)}(F(\Lambda)[1])
 \longrightarrow\operatorname{End}_{\mathrm D(\Gamma)}(\mathbf{Q})=\Lambda'
\]
is precisely $\Phi_\mathbf{P}$.
For $X\in\mathcal H$, Proposition~\ref{prop:chz} gives
$G_0X\in\operatorname{mod}\Lambda$. Adjunction now gives
\[
 \Phi_*\Psi(X)
 \simeq\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm D(E)}(F(\Lambda)[1],p_*X[1])
 \simeq\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm D(\Lambda)}(\Lambda,G_0X)
 \simeq G_0X.
\]
These are isomorphisms of right $\Lambda$-modules. Indeed, for $a\in\Lambda$,
naturality of adjunction identifies precomposition by $\Phi_\mathbf{P}(a)$
with precomposition by left multiplication $l_a$ on $\Lambda$;
for $m:\Lambda\to G_0X$, evaluation at $1$ gives
$(m\circ l_a)(1)=m(a)=m(1)a$.

Since $\Psi$ is essentially surjective, $G_0(\mathcal H)=
\Phi_*(\operatorname{mod}\Lambda')$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:chz}, this is
the intrinsic second-heart image, whose annihilator is
$I_\Lambda(\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{P}))$. Therefore
\[
 I_\Lambda(\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{P}))
 =\operatorname{Ann}_\Lambda\Phi_*(\operatorname{mod}\Lambda')
 =\mathfrak b_\Lambda(\mathbf{P}).
\]
The last assertion follows from \cite[Corollary~4.3]{BZ}.

label: cor:silting-faithfulness-criterion
title: Corollary
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since a module has the same annihilator as the class of its factor
modules and as the class of its submodules,
\[
 J(\mathbf{P})=\operatorname{Ann}_\Lambda\bigl(H^0(\mathbf{P})\oplus H^{-1}(\nu\mathbf{P})\bigr)=0.
\]
Since Lemma~\ref{lem:square-zero-annihilator} gives
$I_1\subseteq J(\mathbf{P})=0$, Lemma~\ref{cor:first-hrs-ideal-silting} gives
$\mathfrak b_\Lambda(\mathbf{P})=0$ and shows that $\mathbf{P}$ is tilting.
head: environment

label: lem:bz-hrs-tower
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{lem:bz-hrs-tower}
\label{cor:bz-ideal-increment}
The silting tower identifies the alternating hearts and their
transported torsion pairs as
\[
 \mathcal{A}^{(2i)}\simeq\operatorname{mod}\Lambda_i,\qquad
 \mathcal{A}^{(2i+1)}\simeq\operatorname{mod} \Gamma_{i},
\]
where $\Lambda_i=\Lambda/I_i$ and the pairs are induced by
$\mathbf{P}_i$ and $\mathbf{Q}_i$, respectively.
Under the composite quotient maps,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:bz-ideal-increment}
 \Lambda_i^{\mathrm{BZ}}=\Lambda_i,\qquad
 I_{i+1}/I_i=\mathfrak b_{\Lambda_i}(\mathbf{P}_i).
\end{equation}
Thus $I_{i+1}=I_i$ if and only if $\mathbf{P}_i$ is tilting.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The first-heart equivalence gives $\mathcal{A}^{(1)}\simeq\operatorname{mod} \Gamma_{0}$.
By Lemma~\ref{cor:first-hrs-ideal-silting}, the second-heart image is
$\operatorname{mod}(\Lambda/\mathfrak b_\Lambda(\mathbf{P}))$.
The transported pair on this quotient is induced by $\mathbf{P}_1$
by \cite[Proposition~3.8]{BZ}.
Theorem~\ref{thm:hrs-ideal-recursion} identifies
$\Lambda/\mathfrak b_\Lambda(\mathbf{P})$ with $\Lambda/I_1$
as quotients of $\Lambda$.
Repeating this argument over $\Lambda_i$ gives
\eqref{eq:bz-ideal-increment}. The last assertion follows from
Lemma~\ref{cor:first-hrs-ideal-silting}.
head: environment

label: thm:hrs-base-change
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $C=\Lambda/J$ and
$\mathbf{P}_C=[P^{-1}/P^{-1}J\xrightarrow{d_C} P^0/ P^0J]$.
By \cite[Corollary~2.4]{Breaz}, $\mathbf{P}_C$ is silting.


Now take $J=\mathfrak b_\Lambda(\mathbf{P})$. Regard $X\in\operatorname{mod}\Lambda_1$ also as a
$\Lambda$-module via the quotient map. Since $\mathbf{P}$ is a bounded
projective complex, tensor--restriction adjunction gives, for $j=0,1$,
\[
 \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm D^{\mathrm b}(\Lambda_1)}(\overline\mathbf{P},X[j])
 \simeq\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm D^{\mathrm b}(\Lambda)}(\mathbf{P},X[j]).
\]
Thus $X$ belongs to $\mathcal{T}(\overline\mathbf{P})$, respectively
$\mathcal{F}(\overline\mathbf{P})$, exactly when its restriction belongs to
$\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{P})$, respectively $\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{P})$.
Set $\mathcal X(\mathbf{Q})=\operatorname{Hom}(\mathbf{Q},\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{Q})[1])$ and
$\mathcal Y(\mathbf{Q})=\operatorname{Hom}(\mathbf{Q},\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{Q}))$.
By \cite[Theorem~4.4]{BZ}, restriction identifies these two classes
with $\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{P})$ and $\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{P})$.
By \cite[Proposition~3.8]{BZ}, $(\mathcal X(\mathbf{Q}),\mathcal Y(\mathbf{Q}))$
is also the pair induced by $\mathbf{P}^+$. Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{eq:base-change-torsion-class}
 (\mathcal{T}(\overline\mathbf{P}),\mathcal{F}(\overline\mathbf{P}))
 =(\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{P}^+),\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{P}^+)).
\end{equation}
The bijection between functorially finite torsion classes and
basic two-term silting complexes \cite[Theorems~2.7 and~3.2]{AIR}
now identifies their basic representatives. Therefore their
additive closures agree, as asserted.
head: environment

label: cor:iterated-hrs-base-change
title: Corollary
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The assertion holds for $i=0$.
Assume it holds at $i$. Theorem~\ref{thm:hrs-base-change}
identifies $\operatorname{add}\mathbf{P}_{i+1}$ with
$\operatorname{add}(\mathbf{P}_i\otimes_{\Lambda_i}\Lambda_{i+1})$.
Since tensor product preserves split summands, we replace $\mathbf{P}_i$ by
$\mathbf{P}\otimes_\Lambda\Lambda_i$ in this equality.
Associativity then gives
$\operatorname{add}\mathbf{P}_{i+1}=\operatorname{add}(\mathbf{P}\otimes_\Lambda\Lambda_{i+1})$.
Since the ideal \eqref{eq: gen-silting} depends only on the additive
closure, \eqref{eq:bz-ideal-increment} gives the formula for each increment.
head: environment

label: prop:exact-parity-stabilization
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By \cite[Corollary~4.3]{BZ}, the Buan--Zhou successor of a tilting
complex is tilting. Hence
\[
 \mathbf{P}_i\text{ tilting}\ \Longrightarrow\ \mathbf{Q}_i\text{ tilting}
 \ \Longrightarrow\ \mathbf{P}_{i+1}\text{ tilting}.
\]
Taking $i=h_{\mathrm{ev}}$ in the first implication and
$i=h_{\mathrm{odd}}$ in the second gives
$h_{\mathrm{odd}}\le h_{\mathrm{ev}}\le h_{\mathrm{odd}}+1$.

The realization $G^{(2i+1)}$ is the forward realization for
$\mathbf{P}_i$. The realization $G^{(2i+2)}$ is backward; shifting its
source heart gives the forward heart for $\mathbf{Q}_i$. Since a shift
is an equivalence, Theorem~\ref{cor:first-hrs-ideal-stopping} and
Lemma~\ref{cor:first-hrs-ideal-silting} give
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 G^{(2i+1)}\text{ is an equivalence}
 &\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \mathbf{P}_i\text{ is tilting}
 \ \Longleftrightarrow\ i\ge h_{\mathrm{ev}},\\
 G^{(2i+2)}\text{ is an equivalence}
 &\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \mathbf{Q}_i\text{ is tilting}
 \ \Longleftrightarrow\ i\ge h_{\mathrm{odd}}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
If $h_{\mathrm{ev}}>0$, the last failing odd index is
$2h_{\mathrm{ev}}-1$.
If $h_{\mathrm{odd}}>0$, the last failing even index is
$2h_{\mathrm{odd}}$.
Taking one more than the last failure gives the maximum in
\eqref{eq:exact-parity-stabilization}.
The same formula gives $1$ when both heights vanish.
Finally,
$h_{\mathrm{ev}}=h_{\mathrm{odd}}$ or
$h_{\mathrm{ev}}=h_{\mathrm{odd}}+1$.
In each case the maximum equals the stated sum.

label: lem:matrix-hrs-ideal
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\mathfrak a$ be the ideal generated by the entries of all
$L\in\ker\Theta_{\mathbf d}$. Given module maps
$u:\Lambda\to P^0$ and
$v:P^{-1}\to\Lambda$, the composite
\[
 \Lambda\xrightarrow{u}\mathbf{P}\xrightarrow{L}\mathbf{P}[-1]
 \xrightarrow{v}\Lambda
\]
is defined by chain maps. By \eqref{eq: gen-silting},
$vLu(1)\in\mathfrak b_\Lambda(\mathbf{P})$. Taking $u(1)=e_i$ in the
$i$th summand of $ P^0$, and taking $v$ to be the projection onto
$f_j\Lambda$ followed by its inclusion into $\Lambda$, gives
$vLu(1)=a_{ji}$. Hence $\mathfrak a\subseteq\mathfrak b_\Lambda(\mathbf{P})$.

Conversely, choose split inclusions of $\mathbf{P}_I$ and $\mathbf{P}_{II}$ in
\eqref{eq: gen-silting} into finite direct sums of $\mathbf{P}$.
Inserting the corresponding projections expresses each generator
of $\mathfrak b_\Lambda(\mathbf{P})$ as a sum of terms $vLu(1)$ as above.
Write $u(1)=(x_i)_i$ and $v(f_j)=y_j$, where
$x_i\in e_i\Lambda$ and $y_j\in\Lambda f_j$. Then
\[
 vLu(1)=\sum_{i,j}y_ja_{ji}x_i\in\mathfrak a.
\]
Thus $\mathfrak b_\Lambda(\mathbf{P})\subseteq\mathfrak a$. Together with
Lemma~\ref{cor:first-hrs-ideal-silting}, this proves
\eqref{eq:matrix-hrs-ideal-equality}.
head: environment

label: lem:hom-id
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
This follows from \cite[Lemmas~2.3(2) and~2.5]{HKM}.
	Explicitly, let $\pi: P^0\twoheadrightarrow H^0(\mathbf{P})$ and
	$\iota:H^{-1}(\mathbf{P})\hookrightarrow P^{-1}$ be the canonical maps.
	A module map $f:H^0(\mathbf{P})\to H^{-1}(\mathbf{P})$ corresponds to the negative
	chain map $L=\iota f\pi$. Conversely, every
	$L: P^0\to P^{-1}$ with $Ld=dL=0$ factors uniquely in this way.
	There are no nonzero homotopies in degree $-1$.
head: environment

label: lem:kernel-first-identities
title: Lemma
head: environment

label: eq:kernel-first-coefficients
title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\pi: P^0\twoheadrightarrow H^{0}(\mathbf{P})$ and
	$\iota:H^{-1}(\mathbf{P})\hookrightarrow P^{-1}$ be the canonical maps.
	Lemmas~\ref{lem:hom-id} and~\ref{lem:matrix-hrs-ideal} give
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:kernel-first-coefficients}
	I=\sum_{\phi:P^{-1}\to\Lambda}\sum_{f:H^{0}(\mathbf{P})\to H^{-1}(\mathbf{P})}
		\phi\iota f(H^{0}(\mathbf{P})).
	\end{equation}
	Thus $I\in\operatorname{Fac} H^{0}(\mathbf{P})=\mathcal{T}$.
	Lemma~\ref{lem:matrix-hrs-ideal} shows that every negative chain
	map $L=\iota f\pi$ has image in $P^{-1}I$.
	Taking the sum of these images gives
	$t(H^{-1}(\mathbf{P}))\subseteq H^{-1}(\mathbf{P})\cap P^{-1}I$.
	
	It remains to prove $ P^0I\subseteq d(P^{-1}I)$.
	A generating term of $ P^0I$ has the form $v\phi L(v')$,
	where $v,v'\in P^0$ and $\phi:P^{-1}\to\Lambda$.
	Set $g(u)=v\phi(u)$.
	Since $\mathbf{P}$ is presilting, there exist
	$X\in\operatorname{End}_\Lambda( P^0)$ and $Y\in\operatorname{End}_\Lambda(P^{-1})$
	with $g=Xd+dY$. Hence
	\[
	v\phi L(v')=gL(v')=dYL(v')\in d(P^{-1}I),
	\]
	since $dL=0$ and $L( P^0)\subseteq P^{-1}I$.
	The reverse inclusion follows from $\Lambda$-linearity.
head: environment

label: thm:main-kernel-filtration
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We first prove $d(P^{-1}I_n)= P^0I_n$ by induction on $n$.
	The case $n=0$ is clear.
	By Corollary~\ref{cor:iterated-hrs-base-change}, $I_{n+1}/I_n$ is the
	first HRS ideal of $\mathbf{P}_n$. Applying Lemma~\ref{lem:kernel-first-identities}
	over $\Lambda_n$ and then using the induction hypothesis gives
	\[
	 P^0I_{n+1}
	=d(P^{-1}I_{n+1})+ P^0I_n
	=d(P^{-1}I_{n+1}).
	\]
	
	The termwise short exact sequence of complexes
	\[
	0\longrightarrow\mathbf{P} I_n\longrightarrow\mathbf{P}
	\longrightarrow\mathbf{P}_n\longrightarrow0,
	\qquad \mathbf{P} I_n=[P^{-1}I_n\xrightarrow d P^0I_n],
	\]
	has $H^0(\mathbf{P} I_n)=0$ and $H^{-1}(\mathbf{P} I_n)=R_n$.
	Its cohomology sequence therefore gives the natural identifications
	in (1) and (2).
	Applying Lemma~\ref{lem:hom-id} to $\mathbf{P}_n$ proves (3), since
	$\Lambda_n$-linear and $\Lambda$-linear maps between these quotient
	modules coincide.  (4) follows from (3).
head: environment

label: rem:kernel-ext-obstruction
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:kernel-ext-obstruction}
	For $n\ge1$, every map $H^{0}(\mathbf{P})\to H^{-1}(\mathbf{P})$ has image in
	$t(H^{-1}(\mathbf{P}))\subseteq R_1\subseteq R_n$ by
	Lemma~\ref{lem:kernel-first-identities}. The connecting map for
	$0\to R_n\to H^{-1}(\mathbf{P})\to H^{-1}(\mathbf{P})/R_n\to0$ therefore yields an isomorphism
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:kernel-ext-description}
		\operatorname{Hom}_\Lambda(H^{0}(\mathbf{P}),H^{-1}(\mathbf{P})/R_n)\xrightarrow[\delta_n]{\sim}
		\ker\bigl[\operatorname{Ext}^1_\Lambda(H^{0}(\mathbf{P}),R_n)\longrightarrow
		\operatorname{Ext}^1_\Lambda(H^{0}(\mathbf{P}),H^{-1}(\mathbf{P}))\bigr].
	\end{equation}
	Since $\delta_n$ is injective, no nonzero map on the left
	lifts to $H^{-1}(\mathbf{P})$.
	By Theorem~\ref{thm:main-kernel-filtration}, these are precisely the
	new negative maps of $\mathbf{P}_n$; their matrix coefficients generate
	$I_{n+1}/I_n$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:matrix-hrs-ideal}.
head: environment

label: prop:main-universal-tilting
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:main-universal-tilting}
	\label{cor:main-two-sided-kernel-bound}
	If $J$ is an ideal of $\Lambda$ and $\mathbf{P}\otimes_\Lambda\Lambda/J$ is tilting,
	then $I_\infty\subseteq J$ and $\Lambda/I_\infty$ is the largest quotient over which
	reduction makes $\mathbf{P}$ tilting.
	Moreover,
	\[
	h_\Lambda(\mathbf{P})\le
	\min\{\ell_\Lambda H^{-1}(\mathbf{P}),
	\ell_{\Lambda^{\mathrm{op}}}\operatorname{Hom}_\Lambda(H^{0}(\mathbf{P}),\Lambda)\}.
	\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Put $h=h_\Lambda(\mathbf{P})$.
	Theorem~\ref{thm:main-kernel-filtration} shows that $\mathbf{P}_h$ is tilting.
	Suppose $\mathbf{P}_J=\mathbf{P}\otimes_\Lambda\Lambda/J$ is tilting.
	We prove $I_n\subseteq J$ by induction. The case $n=0$ is clear.
	Since $I_n\subseteq J$, the quotient map to $\Lambda/J$ factors through
	$\Lambda_n$, and
	\[
	\mathbf{P}_n\otimes_{\Lambda_n}\Lambda/J
	\simeq\mathbf{P}\otimes_\Lambda\Lambda/J=\mathbf{P}_J.
	\]
	The ideal $I_{n+1}/I_n=\mathfrak b_{\Lambda_n}(\mathbf{P}_n)$ is generated by
	the composites in \eqref{eq: gen-silting}, taken over $\Lambda_n$.
	After tensoring with $\Lambda/J$, their middle terms belong to
	$\operatorname{add}\mathbf{P}_J$ and $\operatorname{add}\mathbf{P}_J[-1]$, respectively.
	Since $\mathbf{P}_J$ is tilting, the morphisms between these terms are zero.
	Thus every generating composite maps to zero under
	$\Lambda_n\twoheadrightarrow\Lambda/J$, whose kernel is $J/I_n$.
	It follows that $I_{n+1}/I_n\subseteq J/I_n$, and hence $I_{n+1}\subseteq J$.
	Induction gives $I_\infty\subseteq J$, proving the universal property.
	
	For $n<h$, apply Lemma~\ref{lem:kernel-first-identities} over
	$\Lambda_n$. Under the natural identifications of
	Theorem~\ref{thm:main-kernel-filtration}, it gives
	\[
	0\ne t(H^{-1}(\mathbf{P})/R_n)\subseteq R_{n+1}/R_n.
	\]
	Thus $0=R_0\subsetneq R_1\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq R_h\subseteq H^{-1}(\mathbf{P})$,
	and $h\le\ell_\Lambda H^{-1}(\mathbf{P})$.
	
	Lemma~\ref{lem:kernel-first-identities}  gives $I_{n+1}/I_n\in\mathcal{T}_n=\mathcal{T}$.
	By extension closure, $I_n\in\mathcal{T}=\operatorname{Fac} H^{0}(\mathbf{P})$ for all $n$.
	Since $I_{n+1}$ is generated by images of maps from $H^{0}(\mathbf{P})$,
	$I_n\subsetneq I_{n+1}$ implies
	\[
	\operatorname{Hom}_\Lambda(H^{0}(\mathbf{P}),I_n)\subsetneq\operatorname{Hom}_\Lambda(H^{0}(\mathbf{P}),I_{n+1}).
	\]
	Indeed, equality would force all those images into $I_n$.
	For $0\le n<h$, these form a strict chain of left
	$\Lambda$-submodules of $\operatorname{Hom}_\Lambda(H^{0}(\mathbf{P}),\Lambda)$, proving
	$h\le\ell_{\Lambda^{\mathrm{op}}}\operatorname{Hom}_\Lambda(H^{0}(\mathbf{P}),\Lambda)$.
head: environment

label: thm:main-syzygy-lifting
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{thm:main-syzygy-lifting}
	Let $N=\Omega^2_\Lambda H^{0}(\mathbf{P})$ in a minimal projective resolution of $H^{0}(\mathbf{P})$.
	If every composition factor of $N/t(N)$ belongs to $\mathcal{F}$, then
	$h_\Lambda(\mathbf{P})\le1$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Replace $\mathbf{P}$ by a minimal representative and write
	\[
	\mathbf{P}=[P^{-1}_{\mathrm{pr}}\xrightarrow{d_0} P^0]\oplus W[1],
	\]
	where the first summand is a minimal projective presentation of $H^{0}(\mathbf{P})$
	and $W$ is projective; see \cite[proof of Proposition~3.6]{AIR}.
	Thus $H^{-1}(\mathbf{P})=N\oplus W$.
	Put $I=I_1$ and $S=N\cap P^{-1}_{\mathrm{pr}}I$.
	Then
	\[
	R_1=S\oplus WI,
	\qquad H^{-1}(\mathbf{P})/R_1\simeq(N/S)\oplus(W/WI).
	\]
	Lemma~\ref{lem:kernel-first-identities} gives
	$t(N)\subseteq S$ and $t(W)\subseteq WI$.
	Since $W$ is projective, $WI\in\operatorname{add} I\subseteq\mathcal{T}$; hence
	$WI\subseteq t(W)$ and therefore $WI=t(W)$.
	It follows that $W/WI\in\mathcal{F}$.
	
	The module $N/S$ is a quotient of $N/t(N)$, so all its composition
	factors belong to $\mathcal{F}$. Extension closure of $\mathcal{F}$
	gives $N/S\in\mathcal{F}$.
	Consequently $H^{-1}(\mathbf{P})/R_1\in\mathcal{F}$, and
	Theorem~\ref{thm:main-kernel-filtration} yields $h_\Lambda(\mathbf{P})\le1$.
head: environment

label: cor:collapse
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:collapse}
With $N$ as in Proposition~\ref{thm:main-syzygy-lifting}, if $N$ is semisimple, then
$h_\Lambda(\mathbf{P})\le1$. In particular, when
$\operatorname{rad}^2\Lambda=0$ or $\operatorname{pd}_\Lambda H^{0}(\mathbf{P})\le1$, $N$ is semisimple.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If $N$ is semisimple, so is $N/t(N)\in\mathcal{F}$, and its composition
	factors belong to $\mathcal{F}$ as direct summands.
	If $\operatorname{rad}^2\Lambda=0$, then
	$N\subseteq\operatorname{rad} P^{-1}_{\mathrm{pr}}$ is semisimple.
	If $\operatorname{pd}_\Lambda  H^{0}(\mathbf{P})\le1$, then $N=0$.

title: Example
head: environment

label: prop:nilpotent-silting-realization
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:nilpotent-silting-realization}
	The complex $\mathbf{P}_{\phi}$ is a two-term silting complex over $\Lambda_{\phi}$.  For its
	induced torsion pair
	$(\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{P}_{\phi}),\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{P}_{\phi})),$
	we have
	\[
	J(\mathbf{P}_{\phi})=\mathcal M_{\phi}.
	\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We divide the proof into two steps.
	
	\smallskip
	\noindent\emph{Step 1: $\mathbf{P}$ is a two-term silting complex.}
	Since $\mathbf{P}$ is two-term, to prove that it is presilting it is enough to show
	$\operatorname{Hom}(\mathbf{P},\mathbf{P}[1])=0$.
	Consider the morphism
	\[
	\delta:\operatorname{End}_{\Lambda}(P^0)\oplus\operatorname{End}_{\Lambda}(P^{-1})
	\longrightarrow\operatorname{Hom}_{\Lambda}(P^{-1},P^0),\qquad
	(R,S)\mapsto Rd+dS.
	\]
	There is an isomorphism $\operatorname{Hom}(\mathbf{P},\mathbf{P}[1]) \cong \operatorname{Coker} \delta$.
	
	
	
	
	
	
	Define a $k$-linear map 
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:Psi-definition}
		\Psi:
		M_5(k)\oplus M_3(k)
		\longrightarrow M_{5\times3}(k)^{\oplus2},
		\quad
		(R_0,S_0)\mapsto
		\bigl(R_0A_0+A_0S_0,\,
		R_0C_0+C_0S_0\bigr).
	\end{equation}
	Since $R_Md=dS_M=0$, the map $\delta$ depends only on $R_0,S_0$,
	and hence $\delta=\theta\circ\Psi\circ\pi$.
	
	Since $\pi$ is surjective and $\theta$ is an isomorphism, $\theta$ induces an isomorphism
	$\operatorname{Coker}\Psi
	\xrightarrow{\sim}
	\operatorname{Coker}\delta.$
	Therefore  $\operatorname{Coker} \delta=0 $
	is equivalent to the surjectivity of $\Psi$. 
	The equation
	$\Psi(R_0,S_0)=0$ holds if and only if
	\[
	R_0A_0+A_0S_0=0,
	\qquad
	R_0C_0+C_0S_0=0.
	\]
	After replacing $S_0$ by $-S'_0$, the solutions are precisely
	\[
	R_0=\begin{pmatrix}
	 a&0&0&0&0\\
	 0&a&0&0&0\\
	 b&0&t&0&0\\
	 c&b&0&t&0\\
	 0&c&0&0&t
	\end{pmatrix},\qquad
	S'_0=\begin{pmatrix}
	 a&0&0\\ b&t&0\\ c&0&t
	\end{pmatrix}
	\quad(a,b,c,t\in k).
	\]
	Thus $\dim_k\ker\Psi=4$.
	Since the domain and target have dimensions $34$ and $30$, respectively,
	$\Psi$ is surjective. Therefore $\operatorname{Hom}(\mathbf{P},\mathbf{P}[1])=0$.
	
	
	
	The diagonal blocks corresponding to $\bar X$ and $\bar Y$ give
	$\operatorname{End}_{\mathrm K^{\mathrm b}(\operatorname{proj} B)}(\bar X)=\operatorname{End}_{\mathrm K^{\mathrm b}(\operatorname{proj} B)}(\bar Y)=k$.
	Since $e_1Be_0=0$, homotopies over $B$ vanish, and the different
	projective multiplicities show that $\bar X\not\simeq\bar Y$.
	For $Z=X_\phi,Y_\phi$, reduction modulo $M$ induces a homomorphism
	\[
	\operatorname{End}_{\mathrm K^{\mathrm b}(\operatorname{proj}\Lambda)}(Z)
	\longrightarrow
	\operatorname{End}_{\mathrm K^{\mathrm b}(\operatorname{proj} B)}(Z\otimes_\Lambda B)=k.
	\]
	Since homotopies over $B$ vanish, every element of the kernel has
	a representative with entries in $M$. Since $M^2=0$, the kernel is
	square-zero. Scalar identities lift, so
	$\operatorname{End}_{\mathrm K^{\mathrm b}(\operatorname{proj}\Lambda)}(Z)$ is local.
	Hence $X_\phi,Y_\phi$ are nonisomorphic indecomposables and $\mathbf{P}$ is basic.
	Since $\Lambda$ has exactly two simple modules, we have
	$|\mathbf{P}|=|\Lambda|=2$.  By 
	\cite[Proposition~3.3(b)]{AIR}, a basic two-term presilting complex with
	$|\mathbf{P}|=|\Lambda|$ is silting.  Therefore $\mathbf{P}$ is a basic two-term silting complex.
	
	\smallskip
	\noindent\emph{Step 2: computation of the common annihilator.}
	We first prove that $M$ annihilates $\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{P})=\operatorname{Fac} H^0(\mathbf{P}),$
	and 
	$\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{P})=\operatorname{Sub} H^{-1}(\nu \mathbf{P})$.
	
	For the differential
	$d:P^{-1}\longrightarrow P^0$
	of $\mathbf{P}$, we restrict it to a homomorphism $d_M:P^{-1}M\longrightarrow P^0M.$
	For $X_\phi$, the corner decomposition identifies its restricted differential with
	\[
	V^{\oplus2}\oplus V\xrightarrow{(F_\phi,0)}V^{\oplus2},
	\qquad F_\phi(v,w)=\bigl(w,(1+\phi)v+\phi w\bigr).
	\]
	The last summand $V=e_1Me_1$ maps to zero since $e_0Me_1=0$.
	Since $1+\phi$ is invertible, $F_\phi$ is an isomorphism, with
	\[
	F_\phi^{-1}(a,b)=\bigl((1+\phi)^{-1}(b-\phi a),a\bigr).
	\]
	Hence $H^0(X_\phi)M=0$.
	
	For
	the summand 
	$Y_\phi$ of $\mathbf{P}$,
	the nonzero restriction of $d_M\colon P^{-1}M\to P^0M$ is
	\[
	(e_1Me_0)^{\oplus2}\longrightarrow(e_0Me_0)^{\oplus3},
	\qquad (x,y)\longmapsto(L_\alpha x,L_\beta x+L_\alpha y,L_\beta y).
	\]
	Every $(a,b,c)$ is the image of
	$\bigl(F_\phi^{-1}(a,b),F_\phi^{-1}(0,c)\bigr)$.
	Thus the map is surjective, and
	$H^0(Y_\phi)M=0$
	and 
	$H^0(\mathbf{P})M=0.$
	
	We show that
	$H^{-1}(\nu\mathbf{P})M=0.$
	Let
	$\mathbf{P}^\ast:=\operatorname{Hom}_{\Lambda}(\mathbf{P},\Lambda).$
	Since $\nu\mathbf{P}=D\mathbf{P}^\ast,$
	one has
	$H^{-1}(\nu\mathbf{P})
	\simeq
	D\,H^1(\mathbf{P}^\ast).$
	The nonzero parts of the restricted differentials for $X_\phi^*$
	and $Y_\phi^*$ are
	\[
	(x,y)\longmapsto x\alpha+y\beta,
	\qquad
	(x,y,z)\longmapsto(x\alpha+y\beta,y\alpha+z\beta).
	\]
	They send $(0,(0,a))$ to $a$ and
	$(0,(0,a),(0,b-\phi a))$ to $(a,b)$, respectively.
	Thus both maps are surjective, and the left $\Lambda$-module
	$H^1(\mathbf{P}^*)$ is annihilated by $M$. 
	Thus we obtain
	\[
	M\subseteq
	\operatorname{Ann}_{\Lambda}(\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{P}))\cap\operatorname{Ann}_{\Lambda}(\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{P}))
	=J(\mathbf{P}).
	\]
	
	Conversely, let $\rho:\Lambda\twoheadrightarrow B=\Lambda/M$
	be the quotient map.  Since $M$ annihilates $H^0(X_{\phi})$, this module is
	naturally a $B$-module and identifies with $H^0(\bar X)$.
	Let $x,y$ denote the images of $(e_0,0)$ and $(0,e_0)$ in
	$H^0(\bar X)=\operatorname{Coker}[e_1B\xrightarrow{\binom{\alpha}{\beta}}(e_0B)^2]$.
	They generate its vertex-$0$ component. At vertex $1$, the generators
	are $x\alpha,x\beta,y\alpha,y\beta$, with the sole relation
	$x\alpha+y\beta=0$, since the differential sends $e_1$ to $(\alpha,\beta)$. If $a_0e_0+a_1e_1+b\alpha+c\beta$ annihilates it,
	its action at vertex $1$ gives $a_1=0$. Its action on $x$ gives $a_0x+b x\alpha+c x\beta=0$.
	Since $x$ lies at vertex $0$ and $x\alpha,x\beta$ at vertex $1$,
	the two components vanish separately. Since $x\ne0$ and
	$x\alpha,x\beta$ are linearly independent, $a_0=b=c=0$.
	Thus $H^0(\bar X)$ is faithful over $B$.
	Since $J(\mathbf{P})$ annihilates $H^0(X_{\phi})\in\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{P})$, its
	image $\rho(J(\mathbf{P}))$ annihilates the faithful $B$-module
	$H^0(\bar X)$.  Hence $\rho(J(\mathbf{P}))=0$, and therefore
	$J(\mathbf{P})\subseteq\ker\rho=M.$
	Combining the two inclusions gives $J(\mathbf{P})=M$, as required.

label: prop:nilpotent-first-defect
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We use the matrix description of Lemma~\ref{lem:matrix-hrs-ideal}.  Since
	$P_\phi^{-1}=E_1^3$ and $P_\phi^0=E_0^5$,
	a negative map
	$L:P_\phi^0\longrightarrow P_\phi^{-1}$
	is a $3\times5$ matrix whose entries lie in
	\[
	e_1\Lambda_\phi e_0=e_1\mathcal M_\phi e_0=V^{2}.
	\]
	By \eqref{eq:matrix-defect-kernel} and
	Lemma~\ref{lem:matrix-hrs-ideal}, it is enough to compute the kernel of
	$\Theta_d$ and the ideal generated by its matrix entries.
	
	
	Solving $dL=0$ allows us to write the $j$-th column of $L$ as
	\[
	\kappa_\phi(\mathbf{w}_j)=\bigl(0,(\mathbf{w}_j,0),(\phi \mathbf{w}_j,-(1+\phi)\mathbf{w}_j)\bigr)^{\mathsf t}.
	\]
	For $\mathbf{u}\in V$ the right actions give
	
	\[
	\kappa_\phi(\mathbf{u})\alpha=
	\begin{pmatrix}0\\ \phi \mathbf{u}\\ -\phi \mathbf{u}\end{pmatrix},
	\qquad
	\kappa_\phi(\mathbf{u})\beta=
	\begin{pmatrix}0\\ \phi \mathbf{u}\\ (-1-\phi+\phi^2)\mathbf{u}\end{pmatrix}.
	\]
	Thus
	\[
	\kappa_\phi(\mathbf{u})\alpha+\kappa_\phi(\mathbf{u}')\beta=0
	\iff
	\phi(\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{u}')=0,\quad
	-\phi \mathbf{u}+(-1-\phi+\phi^2)\mathbf{u}'=0.
	\]
	Eliminating $\phi \mathbf{u}$ gives $(1-\phi^2)\mathbf{u}'=0$.  Since $\phi$ is
	nilpotent, $1-\phi^2$ is invertible; hence $\mathbf{u}'=0$ and
	$\mathbf{u}\in\ker\phi$.  Applying this observation to the three equations in
	$Ld=0$ yields
	$\mathbf{w}_2=\mathbf{w}_4=\mathbf{w}_5=0$ and $\phi\mathbf{w}_1=\phi\mathbf{w}_3=0$.
	Hence
	\[
	\ker\Theta_d
	=
	\left\{
	\begin{pmatrix}
		0&0&0&0&0\\
		(\mathbf{w},0)&0&(\mathbf{v},0)&0&0\\
		(0,-\mathbf{w})&0&(0,-\mathbf{v})&0&0
	\end{pmatrix}
	\ \middle|\ \mathbf{w},\mathbf{v}\in\ker \phi
	\right\}
	\simeq(\ker \phi)^{2}.
	\]
	
	
	It remains to determine the coefficient ideal $I_1$ generated by $\ker\Theta_d$.  Put
	$K=\ker\phi$.  The entries of the above matrices generate
	$e_1\mathcal M_\phi(K)e_0=K^{2}.$
	Since $\alpha(0,w)=w$ and $(0,w)\beta=w$ for $w\in K$,
	these entries also generate the two diagonal corners
	\[
	e_0\mathcal M_\phi(K)e_0=K,
	\qquad
	e_1\mathcal M_\phi(K)e_1=K,
	\]
	while $e_0\mathcal M_\phi(K)e_1=0$. Thus this coefficient ideal contains $\mathcal M_{\phi}(K)$.
	Conversely, no larger subspace can be generated by the two-sided actions, since
	$\phi(K)=0$, $\mathcal M_{\phi}^2=0$, and all arrow actions on $e_i\mathcal M_{\phi}e_i$ vanish.  Thus the two-sided ideal generated by the
	matrix entries is exactly
	$\mathcal M_\phi(K).$
	By Lemma~\ref{lem:matrix-hrs-ideal}, we have 
	$I_1=\mathcal M_\phi(\ker\phi).$

label: lem:nilpotent-quotient-compatibility
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:nilpotent-quotient-compatibility}
	Let $U\subseteq V$ be a $\phi$-invariant subspace and let $\bar \phi$ be the induced map on
	$V/U$.  Then $\mathcal M_{\phi}(U)$ is a two-sided ideal of $\Lambda_{\phi}$ and
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:nilpotent-self-similar-quotient}
		\Lambda_{\phi}/\mathcal M_{\phi}(U)\simeq\Lambda_{\bar \phi}.
	\end{equation}
	Under this identification,
	$
	\mathbf{P}_{\phi}\otimes_{\Lambda_{\phi}}
	\Lambda_{\bar\phi}
	\simeq\mathbf{P}_{\bar \phi}.$
	Let $q_U:\Lambda_\phi\twoheadrightarrow\Lambda_{\bar\phi}$ be the
	quotient map under this identification. For every $\phi$-invariant
	subspace $W\supseteq U$, one has
	\[
	q_U(\mathcal M_\phi(W))=\mathcal M_{\bar\phi}(W/U),\qquad
	q_U^{-1}(\mathcal M_{\bar\phi}(W/U))=\mathcal M_\phi(W).
	\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since the arrow actions in \eqref{eq:nilpotent-bimodule-actions} preserve $U$,
	$\mathcal M_{\phi}(U)$ is a $B$--$B$-subbimodule of $\mathcal M_{\phi}$
	and hence a two-sided ideal of $\Lambda_{\phi}$.
	Put $\overline{\mathcal M}=\mathcal M_\phi/\mathcal M_\phi(U)$. Its corners are
	\[
	e_1\overline{\mathcal M}e_0\simeq(V/U)^{\oplus2},\qquad
	e_i\overline{\mathcal M}e_i\simeq V/U\ (i=0,1),\qquad
	e_0\overline{\mathcal M}e_1=0.
	\]
	Let $\pi:V\to V/U$ be the canonical projection. Since
	$\pi\phi=\bar\phi\pi$, these identifications respect the arrow actions,
	so $\overline{\mathcal M}\simeq\mathcal M_{\bar\phi}$ as $B$--$B$-bimodules.
	It follows that
	\[
	\Lambda_\phi/\mathcal M_{\phi}(U)
	\simeq
	B\ltimes(\mathcal M_{\phi}/\mathcal M_{\phi}(U))
	\simeq
	B\ltimes\mathcal M_{\bar\phi}
	=
	\Lambda_{\bar\phi}.
	\]
	
	Since $E_i=e_i\Lambda_\phi$, one has
	$E_i\otimes_{\Lambda_\phi}	\Lambda_{\bar\phi}
	\simeq e_i	\Lambda_{\bar\phi}.$
	Moreover, the quotient map restricts to the identity on
	$B\subseteq\Lambda_\phi$, so the elements $\alpha$ and $\beta$
	remain unchanged.  Therefore
	\[
	X_\phi\otimes_{\Lambda_\phi}	\Lambda_{\bar\phi}
	\simeq
	[	e_1	\Lambda_{\bar\phi}
	\xrightarrow{\binom{\alpha}{\beta}}
	(e_0	\Lambda_{\bar\phi})^{\oplus2}]
	=
	X_{\bar\phi},
	\]
	and similarly 
	$Y_\phi\otimes_{\Lambda_\phi}\Lambda_{\bar \phi}
	\simeq Y_{\bar\phi}.$
	Thus	$\mathbf{P}_\phi\otimes_{\Lambda_\phi}
	\Lambda_{\bar\phi}
	\simeq
	\mathbf{P}_{\bar\phi}.$
	The map $q_U$ is the identity on $B$ and the canonical quotient
	map on each copy of $V$. Since $W\supseteq U$, the image and
	inverse-image formulas follow corner by corner from
	$\pi(W)=W/U$ and $\pi^{-1}(W/U)=W$.

label: thm:nilpotent-operator-defect
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We prove by induction that
	$I_m=\mathcal M_{\phi}(K_m)$ for every $m\ge0$.
	The case $m=0$ follows from $I_0=K_0=0$.
	Assume $I_m=\mathcal M_{\phi}(K_m)$ and let
	$\bar\phi_m$ be the endomorphism induced by $\phi$ on $V/K_m$, namely
	\[
	\bar\phi_m(v+K_m)=\phi(v)+K_m.
	\]
	Its kernel satisfies
	\[
	v+K_m\in\ker\bar\phi_m
	\iff\phi(v)\in K_m
	\iff\phi^{m+1}(v)=0,
	\]
	so $\ker\bar\phi_m=K_{m+1}/K_m$.
	By Lemma~\ref{lem:nilpotent-quotient-compatibility},
	we identify
	\[
	\Lambda_m:=\Lambda_{\phi}/I_m\simeq\Lambda_{\bar \phi_m}.
	\]
	Under this identification, Corollary~\ref{cor:iterated-hrs-base-change} gives
	$I_{m+1}/I_m
	=
	\mathfrak b_{\Lambda_m}
	\bigl(\mathbf{P}_\phi\otimes_{\Lambda_\phi}\Lambda_m\bigr).$
	Hence Proposition~\ref{prop:nilpotent-first-defect} yields
	$I_{m+1}/I_m
	=
	\mathcal M_{\bar\phi_m}(\ker\bar\phi_m).$
	
	Taking inverse images under $q_{K_m}:\Lambda_\phi\twoheadrightarrow\Lambda_m$
	and applying the inverse-image formula in
	Lemma~\ref{lem:nilpotent-quotient-compatibility}, we obtain
	$I_{m+1}=\mathcal M_{\phi}(K_{m+1})$, completing the induction.
	
	For $m<\nu(\phi)$, the nilpotent operator $\bar\phi_m$ acts on the
	nonzero space $V/K_m$, so $\ker\bar\phi_m\ne0$ and
	$K_m\subsetneq K_{m+1}$. For $m\ge\nu(\phi)$, one has $K_m=V$.
	The kernel filtration, and hence the HRS ideal filtration,
	first stabilizes at $\nu(\phi)$, so
	$h_{\Lambda_{\phi}}(\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{P}_{\phi}))=\nu(\phi)$.

label: cor:nilpotent-profile-dimensions
title: Corollary
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Theorem~\ref{thm:nilpotent-operator-defect} gives
	\[
	I_{m+1}/I_m
	\simeq
	\mathcal M_{\bar\phi_m}(\ker\bar\phi_m),
	\quad
	\ker\bar\phi_m\simeq K_{m+1}/K_m.
	\]
	The four corners $e_i\mathcal M_{\bar\phi_m}(\ker\bar\phi_m)e_j$ of $\mathcal M_{\bar\phi_m}(\ker\bar\phi_m)$ are
	\[
	(\ker\bar\phi_m)^{\oplus2},
	\quad
	\ker\bar\phi_m,
	\quad
	\ker\bar\phi_m,
	\quad
	0.
	\]
	Hence
	$\dim_k(I_{m+1}/I_m)
	=
	4\dim_k\ker\bar\phi_m
	=
	4c_m.$
	
	
	Lemma~\ref{lem:nilpotent-quotient-compatibility} and
	Corollary~\ref{cor:iterated-hrs-base-change} give
	$\operatorname{add}\mathbf{P}_m=\operatorname{add}\mathbf{P}_{\bar\phi_m}$
	under the identification
	$\Lambda_m\simeq\Lambda_{\bar\phi_m}$.
	Since both complexes are basic, they are isomorphic in
	$\mathrm K^{\mathrm b}(\operatorname{proj} \Lambda_m)$.
	Proposition~\ref{prop:nilpotent-first-defect} gives
	$\operatorname{Hom}(\mathbf{P}_m,\mathbf{P}_m[-1])\simeq(\ker\bar\phi_m)^{\oplus2}$.
	Hence we have
	\[
	\dim_k\operatorname{Hom}(\mathbf{P}_m,\mathbf{P}_m[-1])=2c_m.
	\]
	Since a two-term silting complex is tilting precisely when its degree $-1$
	self-Hom vanishes, and $c_m=0$ precisely for $m\ge\nu(\phi)$,
	$\mathbf{P}_m$ first becomes tilting at $m=\nu(\phi)$.

label: cor:jordan-profile-realization
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:jordan-profile-realization}
	Let $\lambda=(\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_r\ge1)$ be a
	partition, with conjugate partition $\lambda'$, where
	$\lambda'_j=\#\{i:\lambda_i\ge j\}$. There exist a
	finite-dimensional basic algebra $\Lambda_\lambda$ and a two-term
	silting complex $\mathbf{P}_\lambda$ whose induced torsion pair $(\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{P}_{\lambda}),\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{P}_{\lambda}))$
	satisfies
	$h_{\Lambda_\lambda}(\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{P}_\lambda))=\lambda_1,$
	and, for $0\le m<\lambda_1$,
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:jordan-profile-realization}
		\dim_k(I_{m+1}/I_m)=4\lambda'_{m+1},\quad
		\dim_k\operatorname{Hom}(\mathbf{P}_m,\mathbf{P}_m[-1])=2\lambda'_{m+1}.
	\end{equation}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Take
	$V_\lambda=\bigoplus_{i=1}^r k[z]/(z^{\lambda_i})$
	and let $\phi_\lambda$ be multiplication by $z$.  Set
	$\Lambda_\lambda=\Lambda_{\phi_\lambda}$,
	$\mathbf{P}_\lambda=\mathbf{P}_{\phi_\lambda}$, and  $(\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{P}_{\lambda}),\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{P}_{\lambda}))=(\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{P}_{\phi_\lambda}),\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{P}_{\phi_\lambda}))$.
	Since a block of size $\lambda_i$ contributes $\min(m,\lambda_i)$
	to $\dim_k\ker\phi_\lambda^m$, one has $\nu(\phi_\lambda)=\lambda_1$ and
	\[
	\dim_k\frac{\ker \phi_\lambda^{m+1}}{\ker \phi_\lambda^m}
	=\#\{i\mid\lambda_i\ge m+1\}=\lambda'_{m+1}.
	\]
	Theorem~\ref{thm:nilpotent-operator-defect} and
	Corollary~\ref{cor:nilpotent-profile-dimensions} now give the stated
	height and dimensions.
head: environment

title: Example
body_md:
For a single Jordan block, set
	$V_N=k[z]/(z^N)$ and let $\phi_N$ be multiplication by $z$.
	Write
	\[
	\mathcal M_N:=\mathcal M_{\phi_N},\quad
	\Lambda_N:=\Lambda_{\phi_N},\quad
	\mathbf{P}_N:=\mathbf{P}_{\phi_N},
	\]
	and 
	$(\mathcal{T}_N,\mathcal{F}_N)$ for the corresponding torsion pair.
	
	
	
	
	Since $\ker \phi_N^m=z^{N-m}V_N$ for $0\le m\le N$, Theorem~\ref{thm:nilpotent-operator-defect}
	gives the explicit filtration
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:single-block-defect-chain}
		I_m^{(N)}=\mathcal M_{\phi_N}(z^{N-m}V_N)
		\qquad(0\le m\le N).
	\end{equation}
	The inclusions $I^{(N)}_0\subsetneq I^{(N)}_1\subsetneq\ldots \subsetneq I^{(N)}_N$ are strict and
	$I_N^{(N)}=I_{N+1}^{(N)}=\cdots=\mathcal M_N$.  Moreover, $\dim_k\Lambda_N=\dim_k B+\dim_k\mathcal M_N=4+4N$.
	
	For every $N\ge1$, the single-block family satisfies
	$h_{\Lambda_N}(\mathcal{T}_N)=N$.
	Since $\dim_k(K_{m+1}/K_m)=1$ for $0\le m<N$,
	Corollary~\ref{cor:nilpotent-profile-dimensions} gives
	\[
	\dim_k(I_{m+1}^{(N)}/I_m^{(N)})=4,
	\quad
	\dim_k\operatorname{Hom}(\mathbf{P}_m,\mathbf{P}_m[-1])=2.
	\]
	Thus the HRS height is unbounded even when both dimensions remain fixed
	at every stage before stabilization.

label: cor:minimal-size-height-realization
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{cor:minimal-size-height-realization}
The examples use the least possible number of simple modules.
For height at least two, they also have the least possible Loewy length.

An algebra with one simple module is Morita equivalent to a local
algebra $A$.  Since Morita equivalence transports the HRS iteration,
it preserves height. Thus it suffices to work over $A$.
Represent a two-term silting complex by a minimal complex
$\mathbf{P}=[A^u\xrightarrow d A^v]$; its differential has all entries
in $\operatorname{rad} A$.
Suppose $u,v>0$, and choose a map $A^u\to A^v$ with one entry
$1_A$ and all other entries zero.  This defines a chain map
$\mathbf{P}\to\mathbf{P}[1]$.  Since every entry of a null-homotopic map
$Rd+dS$ belongs to $\operatorname{rad} A$, the chosen map is not null-homotopic.
This contradicts $\operatorname{Hom}(\mathbf{P},\mathbf{P}[1])=0$.  Hence $u=0$ or $v=0$,
and $\mathbf{P}$ is concentrated in one degree.  It is therefore tilting
and has height zero.  Positive height requires at least two
simple modules.

For the second assertion, an algebra of Loewy length at most two
has radical square zero.
Corollary~\ref{cor:collapse} then gives height at most
one.  Hence height at least two requires Loewy length at least three.
The algebras $\Lambda_N$ attain both bounds.
